---
title: "SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3)"
description: "The adjoint action of SU(2) on traceless Hermitian matrices gives a 2-to-1 homomorphism onto SO(3). This is where spin-½ comes from."
date: 2026-11-19
categories: [lie-groups, su(2), so(3), spin]
image: /assets/images/thumbnails/su2-covers-so3.jpg
---

Every physics student learns that a spin-$\half$ state picks up a sign under a
$2\pi$ rotation. The clean statement behind that fact is a homomorphism of Lie
groups
$$
\Phi : \SU(2) \longrightarrow \SO(3), \qquad \ker \Phi = \set{\pm I},
$$ {#eq-double-cover}
which is surjective and exactly two-to-one. This note constructs $\Phi$ and
checks the claims in @eq-double-cover.

## Setting up: rotations as conjugation

Let $\Lie{h}$ denote the real vector space of $2 \times 2$ traceless Hermitian
matrices. It is three-dimensional, with basis the Pauli matrices
$$
\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
so that every $X \in \Lie{h}$ is $X = \vb{x} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}
= x_1 \sigma_1 + x_2 \sigma_2 + x_3 \sigma_3$ for a unique $\vb{x} \in \R^3$.
The key observation is that the ordinary Euclidean length is encoded in the
determinant:
$$
\det(\vb{x} \cdot \boldsymbol\sigma) = -\abs{\vb{x}}^2 .
$$ {#eq-det-norm}

Now let $U \in \SU(2)$ act on $\Lie{h}$ by conjugation,
$$
\Ad_U : X \longmapsto U X U^\dagger .
$$ {#eq-adjoint}
This map is well defined on $\Lie{h}$ — conjugating by a unitary preserves
Hermiticity, and $\Tr(UXU^\dagger) = \Tr(X) = 0$ — and it is linear in $X$.
So $\Ad_U$ is a $3 \times 3$ real matrix in the Pauli basis. Call that matrix
$\Phi(U)$.

::: {#prp-phi-rotation}
For every $U \in \SU(2)$, $\Phi(U) \in \SO(3)$, and
$\Phi : \SU(2) \to \SO(3)$ is a group homomorphism.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Orthogonal.* By @eq-det-norm and multiplicativity of the determinant,
$\abs{\Phi(U)\vb{x}}^2 = -\det(U X U^\dagger) = -\det X = \abs{\vb{x}}^2$,
so $\Phi(U)$ preserves lengths, hence is orthogonal.

*Determinant one.* $\SU(2)$ is connected (it is the $3$-sphere, see
@rem-s3), and $U \mapsto \det \Phi(U)$ is a continuous map into
$\set{\pm 1}$ that takes the value $1$ at $U = I$. So it is identically $1$.

*Homomorphism.* $\Ad_{UV}(X) = UVX(UV)^\dagger = U(VXV^\dagger)U^\dagger
= \Ad_U \Ad_V (X)$, so $\Phi(UV) = \Phi(U)\Phi(V)$.
:::

::: {#rem-s3}
## $\SU(2)$ is a 3-sphere

Writing $U = \begin{pmatrix} a & -\bar b \\ b & \bar a \end{pmatrix}$ with
$a, b \in \C$, the condition $\det U = 1$ becomes $\abs{a}^2 + \abs{b}^2 = 1$,
which is the unit sphere $S^3 \subset \C^2 \iso \R^4$. In particular $\SU(2)$
is compact, connected and simply connected — the last property is exactly what
$\SO(3)$ lacks, and is why one of them covers the other and not the reverse.
:::

## The kernel

::: {#thm-kernel}
$\ker \Phi = \set{I, -I} \iso \Z/2\Z$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$U \in \ker\Phi$ means $UXU^\dagger = X$, i.e. $U$ commutes with every traceless
Hermitian matrix. Since every $2\times 2$ matrix is a complex linear combination
of $I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$, such a $U$ commutes with *all* $2 \times 2$
matrices, hence is a scalar $\lambda I$ (Schur's lemma, or a direct check).
Then $\det U = \lambda^2 = 1$ forces $\lambda = \pm 1$. Conversely $\pm I$
clearly act trivially.
:::

## Surjectivity, and what a $2\pi$ rotation does

A direct calculation with $U = \exp(-i\theta\, \hat{\vb n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2)$
shows that $\Phi(U)$ is the rotation by angle $\theta$ about the unit axis
$\hat{\vb n}$:
$$
\Phi\!\left(e^{-i\theta\, \hat{\vb n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2}\right)
= R_{\hat{\vb n}}(\theta).
$$ {#eq-rotation}
Since every rotation has this form, $\Phi$ is surjective, and by the first
isomorphism theorem $\SO(3) \iso \SU(2)/\set{\pm I}$.

Now set $\theta = 2\pi$ in @eq-rotation. The right-hand side is the identity
rotation. The left-hand side is $\exp(-i\pi\, \hat{\vb n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)
= \cos\pi\, I - i \sin\pi\, \hat{\vb n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma = -I$. The two
elements of $\SU(2)$ sitting over a given rotation are $U$ and $-U$, and a full
turn takes you from one to the other.

::: {.callout-important}
## The physical content

A quantum state is a ray in a Hilbert space $\hilb$, so overall phases are
unobservable, and a "representation" of the rotation group on $\hilb$ only
needs to hold up to phase. Such projective representations of $\SO(3)$ are the
same thing as honest representations of its universal cover $\SU(2)$. The
representations of $\SU(2)$ that do *not* descend to $\SO(3)$ — the ones where
$-I$ acts as $-1$ rather than $+1$ — are precisely the half-integer spins. So
the existence of fermions is, at bottom, the statement that $\pi_1(\SO(3)) =
\Z/2\Z$.
:::

## Checks and loose ends

- The Lie algebra version of @eq-double-cover is an *isomorphism*
  $\su(2) \iso \so(3)$: the kernel is discrete, so it is invisible to the
  tangent space at the identity. Covering maps are always Lie algebra
  isomorphisms.
- The same construction with $\SL(2,\C)$ acting on *all* $2 \times 2$ Hermitian
  matrices (now including the identity direction, which carries the time
  component) gives the double cover $\SL(2,\C) \to \SO^+(1,3)$ of the proper
  orthochronous Lorentz group. That is the origin of Weyl spinors.
- For the general theory of covering groups see Hall [@hall2015, ch. 1 and 5];
  for the physics see Woit [@woit2017, ch. 6] and Schwichtenberg
  [@schwichtenberg2018, ch. 3].
